frase_gancho.texto: A young man of green stone holds a sleeping child with jaguar features.

puente_narrativo.texto: Jade was also used to bury offerings. Look for a group of green figures facing each other in a circle, in front of a row of axes, as if someone had frozen a meeting in time.

guion_corto.texto: You are standing before the exact-scale reproduction of the famous Lord of Las Limas. The original sculpture, carved in green serpentine, fifty-five centimeters tall and weighing sixty kilograms, and now kept in the Xalapa Museum of Anthropology, was found in the town of Las Limas, in Veracruz. It portrays a young man seated with his legs crossed, holding in his arms a limp child with jaguar features: the mouth with downturned corners, the slanted eyes. Look at the young man’s shoulders and knees: they bear small engraved figures, faces in profile that can be read as four Olmec gods. That is why this piece has been called a treatise on religion in stone. Is the child asleep? Is he an offering? Is he a god? No one knows for certain.

guion_largo.texto:
Sometimes the discovery is as interesting as the piece itself. According to the story, in 1965 some children from the town of Las Limas, in Veracruz, found this green stone and took it for an ordinary rock. When they saw the carved face, the villagers believed it was an apparition of the Virgin: they covered it with flowers on a makeshift altar and venerated it as “the Virgin of Las Limas” before it passed into archaeological custody in Xalapa. A sacred image from three thousand years ago, received as a new sacred image.

Look at it closely. A young man, seated with his legs crossed, carries in his arms a child who seems to be sleeping, or without strength. The child has jaguar features: the slanted eyes and the mouth with downturned corners, the same mouth you already saw in the baby faces of Tlapacoya and Tlatilco. Specialists sometimes call him a “man-jaguar,” and here we see him as a child. What makes him so important? That he brings together in a single image a human being and the most powerful beast of the jungle.

The jaguar returns once again, and this is where it begins. You saw it on the Toltec frieze, in the warriors and gods of Teotihuacán, and as the Ocelotl in the Mexica Hall. Here it appears more than two thousand years before the Mexica, and everything suggests that it was already the most powerful animal in the imagination. There is a famous theory, still debated, according to which the Olmec told of themselves as descendants of the union between a woman and a jaguar. Perhaps this child is that memory.

Now, notice the small drawings engraved on the stone: one on each shoulder and one on each knee. They are faces in profile, and specialists read them as the four great gods of the Olmec world: they have been linked to fire, maize, sky, and earth. It is as if the sculptor had left, in the margins of the image, the notes of an encyclopedia of his religion. That is why this piece is said to be a visual treatise.

The material speaks too. Green stone, for the Olmec, was water, life, and young maize, like the jade of the Zapotec bat mask. This block was polished with sand and patience until it became smooth as a mirror. It measures fifty-five centimeters, yet it commands attention like a monumental sculpture: it is among the largest and finest works in green stone from the entire Olmec culture.

And the child? There is no single answer. Some think he is asleep, in a trance; some see him as an offering, and some believe he is a child god. Perhaps the ambiguity is part of its power. What we do see is something deeply human: an adult carefully holding a fragile creature. Three thousand years later, that gesture still feels close to us, and perhaps that is why this piece moves even those who have never heard of the Olmec.

texto.Material: Museum reproduction at 1:1 scale (the original is incised green serpentine and is kept in the Xalapa Museum of Anthropology, Veracruz)
texto.Origin: Las Limas, municipality of Jesús Carranza, Veracruz
texto.Dimensions: 55 cm high x 42 cm wide x 33 cm thick
texto.Discovery: July 16, 1965, by the children Severiano and Rosa Manuel Pascual

texto.pregunta: Myth: It is a Virgin and Child, as the villagers who found it believed.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a young Olmec man with a jaguar child, sculpted about three thousand years ago, long before the arrival of the Spanish.
